title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Kutuzov fell back toward Vienna, destroying the bridges over the River Inn at Braunau and the River Traun near Linz as he went. On October 23, the Russian troops were crossing the River Enns. By midday, the Russian baggage train, artillery, and columns of troops were filing through the town of Enns on both sides of the bridge.

It was a warm, rainy autumn day. The wide landscape that opened out below the heights where the Russian batteries guarded the bridge was sometimes veiled by a sheer curtain of slanting rain, and then suddenly revealed in sunlight, with far-off objects glittering as if freshly varnished. Down below, the little town could be seen with its white, red-roofed houses, its cathedral, and its bridge, on both sides of which masses of Russian troops were streaming and jostling. At the bend of the Danube, boats, an island, and a castle with a park stood visible, surrounded by the waters where the Enns flowed into the Danube. The rocky left bank of the Danube was covered with pine forests, with a mysterious backdrop of green treetops and bluish ravines. The towers of a convent rose beyond a stretch of untouched pine forest, and far away on the other side of the Enns, enemy cavalry patrols could be spotted.

On the brow of the hill, among the field guns, the general commanding the rearguard stood with a staff officer, scanning the countryside through his field glass. A little behind them sat Nesvitski, who had been sent to the rearguard by the commander in chief, perched on the trail of a gun carriage. A Cossack who accompanied him had handed over a knapsack and flask, and Nesvitski was treating some officers to pies and genuine doppelkümmel liqueur. The officers had gathered around him gladly, some on their knees, others squatting cross-legged on the wet grass.
"Yes, the Austrian prince who built that castle was no fool. Lovely place! Why aren't you eating, gentlemen?" Nesvitski was saying.

"Thank you very much, Prince," answered one of the officers, pleased to be chatting with such an important staff officer. "It really is a lovely place! We passed right by the park and spotted two deer... and what a magnificent house!"

"Look, Prince," said another officer, who would have loved to take another pie but felt too self-conscious and so pretended to be studying the landscape. "See—our infantry have already made it over there. Look, in the meadow behind the village, three of them are dragging something. They'll clean out that castle," he observed with obvious approval.
"I'm sure they will," said Nesvitski. "No, but what I'd really love," he added, munching a pie with his moist-lipped, handsome mouth, "would be to slip in over there."
He pointed with a grin toward a turreted convent, his eyes narrowing and gleaming.
"Now that would be something, gentlemen!"
The officers laughed.
"Just to ruffle the nuns a bit. I hear there are Italian girls among them. I swear I'd give five years of my life for it!"
"They must be pretty bored too," said one of the bolder officers with a laugh.
Meanwhile, the staff officer up front pointed something out to the general, who looked through his field glass.

"Yes, that's right, that's right," the general said irritably, lowering his field glass and shrugging. "That's right! They'll come under fire at the crossing. And why are they dragging their feet over there?"

On the far side, the enemy was visible to the naked eye, and a milky-white cloud of smoke rose from their battery. Then came the distant boom of a shot, and the Russian troops could be seen rushing toward the crossing.
Nesvitski heaved himself up, puffing, and walked over to the general with a smile.
"Wouldn't your excellency care for a little refreshment?" he offered.
"It's a bad business," the general replied without acknowledging the offer. "Our men have wasted too much time."
"Shall I ride over there, your excellency?" Nesvitski asked.

"Yes, please do," the general answered, and repeated the detailed order that had already been given once before: "And tell the hussars they are to cross last and set fire to the bridge, as I ordered. And the inflammable material on the bridge needs to be inspected again."
"Very good," Nesvitski replied.
He called over the Cossack with his horse, told him to stow the knapsack and flask, and swung his heavy frame easily into the saddle.
"I really will stop by the convent," he told the officers, who watched him with smiles, and he rode off down the winding path along the hillside.
"Now then, Captain, let's see how far it'll carry. Give it a try!" said the general, turning to an artillery officer. "A bit of fun to pass the time."
"Crew, to your guns!" the officer commanded.
In a moment the men came running cheerfully from their campfires and began loading.
"Fire!" came the command.

Number one jumped nimbly aside. The gun roared with a deafening metallic blast, and a whistling shell flew over the heads of the troops below the hill before landing well short of the enemy, a small puff of smoke marking where it burst.

The faces of officers and soldiers alike brightened at the sound. Everyone stood up and began watching the movements of the Russian troops below—as clearly visible as if they were only a stone's throw away—and the approaching enemy further off. At that same moment, the sun broke fully through the clouds, and the sharp crack of the solitary shot merged with the brilliance of the bright sunshine into one joyful, exhilarating impression.
